Suing Someone for Assault in Washington: The Two-Year Deadline, the Criminal Case, and Who Actually Pays

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·8 min read·November 11, 2026

A man you had never met hit you from behind outside a bar in downtown Spokane, and you spent the night in the emergency room with a broken orbital bone. He was arrested, the prosecutor's office has sent you a letter, and you assume the case is being taken care of. The criminal case belongs to the state, though, and its job is to punish him. Whether you are ever paid for the surgery, the lost work, and the months of double vision is a separate case that only you can bring, and Washington gives you less time to bring it than it gives for almost any other injury.

Can I sue someone who assaulted me in Washington?

Yes. Assault and battery are civil wrongs as well as crimes, and the person hurt can sue for damages. Washington's limitation statutes list them by name as civil actions, which is where the trouble starts, because they are given a deadline of their own.

The civil case and the criminal case can come out of the same five seconds of violence and have almost nothing else in common: not the parties, not the rules of proof, not the deadline, and not what you get at the end.

How long do I have to sue for assault?

Two years. RCW 4.16.100(1) requires an action for libel, slander, assault, assault and battery, or false imprisonment to be brought within two years. That is shorter than the three years RCW 4.16.080(2) allows for most other injuries to the person, and it is the number people get wrong, because three years is the figure everybody has heard.

The two years runs regardless of the criminal case. A prosecution that takes eighteen months to reach trial can use up nearly all of it before anyone thinks about a lawsuit.

RCW 4.16.190 takes out of the limitation period the time a person was under eighteen when the claim accrued, or incompetent or disabled to the degree that they cannot understand the nature of the proceedings. A child's claim does not expire on the adult schedule.

Sexual abuse of a child has its own statute. RCW 4.16.340 governs claims based on intentional conduct for injury from childhood sexual abuse. For abuse that occurred before June 6, 2024, it allows the latest of several three-year periods, including three years from when the victim discovered that the act caused the injury, and the time does not run until the child turns eighteen. For abuse on or after June 6, 2024, subsection (6) says there is no time limit at all.

A claim against someone else on a different theory, such as negligence by a property owner or an employer, may run on a different clock. That is one more reason to have the deadline worked out early rather than assumed.

The criminal case and your civil case are not the same thing

The prosecutor represents the State of Washington. You are a witness in that case, and an important one, but you do not decide whether charges are filed, whether a plea deal is offered, or what the sentence is. In the civil case you are the plaintiff. You decide whether to sue, whom to sue, whether to settle, and for how much.

The criminal case also carries its own burden of proof. RCW 9A.04.100(1) says no person may be convicted of a crime unless each element is proved by competent evidence beyond a reasonable doubt. That standard is written for criminal convictions. A prosecutor who declines to charge because a case cannot be proved beyond a reasonable doubt has made a decision about the criminal case, not about yours.

The two cases still affect each other. What you tell police becomes evidence, and a defendant facing charges will often refuse to answer questions in a civil case until the criminal one is over. When to file is a decision to make deliberately.

Restitution is not compensation

If the person is convicted, the court will usually order restitution. RCW 9.94A.753(5) says restitution shall be ordered whenever the offender is convicted of an offense that results in injury to any person, unless extraordinary circumstances make it inappropriate.

What it covers is narrow, and the statute says so. RCW 9.94A.753(3)(a) limits restitution to easily ascertainable damages for injury to or loss of property, actual expenses incurred for treatment for injury to persons, and lost wages resulting from injury. Restitution shall not include reimbursement for damages for mental anguish, pain and suffering, or other intangible losses, though it may include the costs of counseling reasonably related to the offense.

RCW 9.94A.753(9) is the other half: the section does not limit civil remedies or defenses available to the victim. Restitution and a civil claim run side by side. Accepting restitution does not settle the civil case, and a restitution order says nothing about whether the person who owes it will ever pay.

Crime victims' compensation, and the deadlines on it

Washington runs a crime victims' compensation program through the Department of Labor and Industries under chapter 7.68 RCW. It can pay medical bills and part of lost wages while everything else is unresolved. RCW 7.68.070(1) makes a victim injured as a result of a criminal act eligible for benefits within the program's limits, and except for medical benefits, no more than forty thousand dollars may be granted for a single injury or death.

There are two deadlines, and the first is the one that catches people. Under RCW 7.68.060(1)(b), no compensation is available if the criminal act was not reported to a local police department or sheriff's office within twelve months, or, if it could not reasonably have been reported in that time, within twelve months of when it reasonably could have been. Under RCW 7.68.060(1)(a), the application itself must be received by the department within three years after the act was reported to police, which the department may extend for good cause to as much as five years.

There are conditions as well. RCW 7.68.060(3) makes a person ineligible who refuses reasonable cooperation with law enforcement, with exceptions for age, health, language barriers, and safety. RCW 7.68.060(2)(a) bars benefits where the injury resulted from consent, provocation, or incitement by the victim. And RCW 7.68.130 makes the program secondary to other insurance: victims must use their private insurance first, and benefits are reduced by other public or private insurance available.

The program and a lawsuit are not alternatives. RCW 7.68.050(1) says no right of action for damages is lost because a person is entitled to these benefits. If you recover from the person who hurt you, though, RCW 7.68.050(10) gives the department a lien on the recovery for its share, and RCW 7.68.050(21) makes a settlement that results in less than the victim's entitlement void unless the department approves it in writing. Settling a civil claim without dealing with the department can undo the settlement.

Will the attacker's insurance pay?

Often this is the real question, because a judgment against a person with no assets and no insurance is a piece of paper. People reasonably assume that a homeowner's or renter's policy will respond to an assault by the policyholder or on the property. Liability policies commonly exclude injury the insured expected or intended, and an assault is the kind of act those exclusions are written for.

Whether a particular policy covers a particular incident depends on its wording and the facts, and it is not something to assume in either direction. It is answered by reading the actual policy, which first means getting a copy.

Can I sue the bar, the landlord, or the employer?

Sometimes the person who threw the punch is not the only one responsible, and sometimes they are. A claim against a business, a property owner, or an employer for failing to provide reasonable security, or for failing to supervise an employee, is a negligence claim with its own requirements. Whether one exists depends heavily on the relationship between the parties and on what the business knew or should have known before the attack.

The facts that decide it are the ones that disappear fastest: earlier incidents at the location, how many staff were working that night, whether security or a manager had been warned about the person, what the cameras recorded, and whether the attacker was on the job at the time. If any of that is in play, the evidence has to be requested in the first weeks, not near the end of the two years.

What if the person who assaulted me was a police officer?

Force used by an on-duty officer is usually a different case, brought as an excessive force claim under the Fourth Amendment and 42 U.S.C. section 1983, often with state law claims alongside it. It has its own immunity rules, and a state law claim against a city, county, or the state requires a tort claim to be presented before suit. The article on section 1983 civil rights claims in Washington covers the federal side, and the article on claims against government entities covers the claim filing step.

Where this goes wrong

The victim relies on the three-year deadline they have heard about for injury claims, and the two years under RCW 4.16.100(1) runs out first.

The family waits for the criminal case to finish and assumes restitution will make them whole, then learns at sentencing that RCW 9.94A.753(3)(a) excludes pain and suffering entirely.

Nobody files a police report, or it is filed late, and the twelve-month reporting requirement in RCW 7.68.060(1)(b) closes off crime victims' compensation.

A civil settlement is signed without involving the Department of Labor and Industries, and the department's lien and approval rights under RCW 7.68.050 come back to the victim afterward.

The bar's video is overwritten before anyone asks for it, and with it the evidence of what staff saw.

The victim sues only the attacker, who has nothing, and nobody looks at whether a business, an employer, or an insurance policy might respond.

What a lawyer does here

Most of the early work protects deadlines and evidence. Calculating the two-year limitation period and any tolling. Making sure the police report exists and the crime victims' compensation application goes in on time. Getting the criminal file. Sending preservation demands to any business or landlord before the video is gone. Finding out whether there is insurance and getting the policy. And resolving the department's lien so that a settlement actually holds.
